big_case.notes: Plenary Supreme Court grant on the pleading and liability standard for misleading omissions of intra-quarter financial data under Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933. Carrying significant practical consequences for IPO registration statements, underwriter liability, and federal securities class-action litigation nationwide, though narrowed to reformulated Question 1 (excluding Item 303) and confined to statutory securities disclosure law rather than broad constitutional or structural questions.

central_claims.basis: After the Solicitor General filed its invited brief on October 7, 2026, both sides filed supplemental briefs on October 20-21, the petition was redistributed on October 21 for the November 6 Conference and relisted once on November 9 for the November 13 Conference (total distribution_count 3, with no second CVSG), though the SG filed in early October rather than late November or December.
central_claims.claim: Once the Solicitor General files its brief, the petition will be redistributed with party supplemental briefs and resolved at the first post-SG conference or after at most one relist, with no second CVSG.

central_claims.basis: The Solicitor General's October 7, 2026 brief argued that the Ninth Circuit erred on Section 11(a)'s misleading-omissions inquiry and recommended granting certiorari on Question 1, and the Court granted review on November 13, 2026.
central_claims.claim: The petition is slightly more likely than not to be granted, tracking an expected Solicitor General brief criticizing the Ninth Circuit's expansive disclosure analysis.

central_claims.basis: The November 13, 2026 order granted certiorari limited solely to Question 1 as reformulated by the Solicitor General and declined Question 2; the primary call that both questions would be taken essentially as written did not hold, although the document accurately identified Question 1 as the cleaner post-Macquarie vehicle and the likelier narrowing if the SG counseled one.
central_claims.claim: If granted, the Court will most likely take both questions presented essentially as written, though Question 1 is the cleaner vehicle and a grant limited to Question 1 alone is the likelier narrowing if the Solicitor General counsels a narrower grant.
